I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessing domestic violence, the trigger pattern is strongly male-linked ('being alone with men') but also includes 'being alone with women' without any corresponding formulation or symptom content explaining why both genders would be equivalently triggering. That broadens the trigger profile in a way that is hard to connect to the rest of the report, which is centered on interpersonal threat from others who might harm him rather than gender-nonspecific social presence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Driving/being a passenger in a vehicle' is difficult to link to the reported trauma and the rest of the profile. No other trigger, threat, or memory item involves transport, accidents, escape, or vehicles, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain not represented elsewhere in the five components.

vignette: Tane, an 18‑year‑old project manager at a small tech startup in a coastal town, arrived at the clinic with a quiet urgency. When he was eight, his mother’s voice had cracked as his father raised a wooden chair, the chair striking her chest. The room had smelled of stale beer and sweat; a sudden, blaring crash echoed the beat of his father’s fists. Tane later remembered the slam of the door, the scrape of his mother’s head against the sofa, and the sound of a man’s laugh that seemed to echo in the hallway. Those moments were never a clean narrative; he could only piece together fragments—an incomplete picture that flickered in the back of his mind. The memory of the night still erupted with terror when it surfaced, yet it always felt unfinished, as if a part of the story had been smudged. When a male colleague enters his office or when he rides his bicycle to work, the scent of alcohol on a passer‑by’s breath, or the faint odor of a night out, the incomplete memory flares, and he feels the same rush of dread that held him as a child. Those triggers set off a chain of alarm: he immediately checks that all doors are locked, his ears sharpen to the thud of distant footsteps, and his eyes scan coworkers for any hint of menace. The startle response to ordinary sounds—like the squeak of a keyboard—forces him to pause and re‑verify that the office is safe. The mere presence of men in his surroundings intensifies this threat vigilance, turning every male figure into a potential danger. The awareness that a threat might lurk in the doorway makes the incomplete memories grow even more salient, reinforcing the loop between trigger and memory. The same triggers and memory fragments also push Tane toward maladaptive strategies. When a male presence makes him uneasy, he often reaches for a cigarette, inhaling the tobacco smoke as if it might smother the echo of a child’s fear. Alcohol and prescription medication sometimes find their way into his nightly routine, offering a temporary numbness that dissolves the racing heart that follows each lock check. He avoids people, especially men, in the office, preferring to sit alone in a corner or leave the room entirely. The bicycle, a symbol of movement, is an immediate trigger—once the wind rushes past him, the memory of a father’s fist feels like it is behind him again. He has stopped biking altogether, choosing the bus instead, a decision that costs him both time and reputation. In the quiet of his apartment, he watches the television, then shifts his gaze to the window, watching other people walk by as if to anticipate a threat. Each time the memory of terror on recall surfaces, he feels compelled to smoke or drink to regain a sense of control, even though these substances ultimately heighten his perception of danger. The threat of an attack—real or imagined—feeds his avoidance of male colleagues, which in turn intensifies the sense of isolation that makes his threat responses more acute. The maladaptive strategies that arise from the triggers and memory, in turn, reinforce the threat perception. Tane’s smoking raises his pulse, which sharpens his startle reflex and makes him even more vigilant. The act of checking doors becomes a ritual after he has inhaled a cigarette, as he believes that the nicotine dulls the terror that might otherwise overwhelm him. After a startle incident, he may turn to alcohol, believing it will smooth the edges of the fragmented memories that swirl in his mind. These substances do not calm his anxiety; instead, they amplify his hyperarousal, forcing him to watch every face for signs of harm. He often observes coworkers from a distance, hoping that a distant gaze will prevent a potential threat. The more he watches, the more convinced he becomes that he must be ready for violence. This continuous monitoring, fueled by his own strategies, perpetuates the cycle of threat, memory, and avoidance. Now, Tane is at a crossroads. His relationship has begun to suffer, as he refuses to accept his partner’s male friends at dinner, fearing they might be predators. At work, he misses deadlines and avoids important meetings because the very act of stepping into a room feels like walking into a danger zone. The avoidance has begun to erode his professional reputation and threaten his job stability. He decided to seek help because the daily routine of checking locks, smoking, and watching others has become unsustainable. He is terrified of losing his relationship and his career, yet he also hopes to reclaim the parts of his life that feel safe and intact. The last thing that pushed him to the clinic was a night of restless sleep, the constant whisper of his heart in his ears, and the realization that his avoidance had become a prison rather than a shield.
